title: Hollywood Video (1988–2010): post-mortem · Spectre Brands
description: From 25 stores to 2,006, a near-collapse in 2000, a three-way takeover fight and a buyer that borrowed too much. Drawn from the SEC filings of Hollywood Entertainment and Movie Gallery.

card.blurb: The No. 2 video rental chain survived its own dot-com disaster, then was sold in 2005 to a rival that paid mostly with borrowed money. Five years later every store was in liquidation.

stat.label: merger value in April 2005; liquidation was approved five years later

hero.dates: First store opened Oct 1988. Liquidation of the last stores approved May 2010.
hero.standfirst: It got through the mistake it made itself. It did not get through the one its buyer made.
hero.deck: Hollywood Entertainment grew from 25 video stores at the end of 1993 to 1,615 six years later, bought a web retailer at the top of the bubble, and by the end of 2000 its auditors doubted it could continue. It recovered, and by 2004 had 2,006 stores and three suitors. The winner, Movie Gallery, paid with borrowed money just as renters began to drift to the mailbox and the kiosk. Its sources are the two companies’ SEC filings and the wire reports of the 2010 liquidation.

findings.title: It grew faster than it could pay for.
findings.text: Stores went from 25 at the end of 1993 to 1,615 at the end of 1999, and long-term obligations from $8.0M in 1995 to $533.9M in 1999.[^1][^2]

findings.title: Its dot-com bet lasted 20 months.
findings.text: Hollywood bought Reel.com for about $96.9M on October 1, 1998 and closed its e-commerce business on June 12, 2000, with a $69.3M charge.[^3]

findings.title: It recovered before it was sold.
findings.text: After a restated net loss of $548.3M in 2000, the company reported four straight profitable years and revenue of $1.78B in 2004.[^5]

findings.title: The highest bid did not win.
findings.text: Blockbuster offered $14.50 a share in cash and stock. The board took Movie Gallery’s $13.25 in cash, which cleared antitrust review quickly.[^8][^9]

findings.title: The buyer wrote the brand down to almost nothing.
findings.text: Movie Gallery impaired $361.2M of Hollywood Video goodwill in 2005 and cut the trademark’s value to $15.0M during 2007.[^11][^13]
